entries.question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate is incorrect — state-based actions cause the Saga to be sacrificed before triggers are placed on the stack, so Eternal Witness’s triggered ability can target Elspeth Conquers Death in the graveyard.
entries.answer:
No — Eternal Witness cannot target Elspeth Conquers Death.

Elspeth Conquers Death's chapter III ability is a triggered ability that returns a target creature or planeswalker card from your graveyard to the battlefield. Eternal Witness enters during that ability's resolution, and its own triggered ability ("When this creature enters, you may return target card from your graveyard to your hand") chooses its target as it's put on the stack, the next time a player would receive priority (rules 115.1d, 603.3d). At that moment Elspeth Conquers Death has not gone to the graveyard — a Saga's "Sacrifice after III" happens only after the chapter III ability has left the stack, so during and immediately after the resolution of chapter III the Saga is still a permanent on the battlefield. A card in your graveyard is the only legal target for Eternal Witness's ability, so Elspeth Conquers Death is not a legal choice; you'd pick some other card in your graveyard (or, since the ability says "you may," decline on resolution).

Timing note: I'm assuming the normal sequence — chapter III resolves fully (Eternal Witness enters), then Eternal Witness's trigger goes on the stack, and the Saga's sacrifice is put on the stack at that same time rather than earlier. If somehow Elspeth Conquers Death were already in your graveyard when Eternal Witness's trigger was put on the stack, it would be a legal target then; that's exactly the principle behind Eternal Witness ruling #0, which says Eternal Witness's ability can target a card that hits your graveyard as the resolving spell that put Eternal Witness onto the battlefield finishes resolving. The specific rules governing when a Saga is sacrificed after its final chapter were not included in the context provided here, so treat that part as the standard Saga behavior described on the card ("Sacrifice after III").

Nothing here depends on the number of players: the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table (Elspeth Conquers Death's chapter I targeting "a permanent an opponent controls" would matter for multiplayer, but chapter III only looks at your own graveyard).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

When the final chapter ability resolves, Eternal Witness is returned to the battlefield. However, its triggered ability is not put onto the stack until after state based actions are checked. When state based actions are checked, Elspeth Conquers Death is sacrificed because is has a number of lore counters greater than or equal to its final chapter number. After this, triggers are placed onto the stack, and Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard able to be the target of Eternal Witness's triggered ability.

entries.question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same correct conclusion that Robber of the Rich lets Autumn spend {C} as red mana to pay Light Up the Stage's {R} spectacle cost (if spectacle is available).
entries.answer:
Yes — Autumn can pay the {R} spectacle cost using a single {C}, provided an opponent has actually lost life this turn.

Why: Robber of the Rich says that during any turn you attacked with a Rogue, you may cast the exiled card "and you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." That lets Autumn treat one colorless mana ({C}) as red mana for the purpose of paying Light Up the Stage's cost. Per 609.4b, an effect that lets you spend mana "as though it were mana of any color" affects only how you may pay a cost — it doesn't change the cost itself and doesn't change what mana was actually spent. So the cost paid is still the spectacle cost of {R}, satisfied by {C}.

Spectacle (702.137a) is a static ability that works on the stack: "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn." It's an alternative cost announced during casting (601.2b, 601.2f), so Autumn announces they're paying spectacle {R} instead of the normal {2}{R}, then pays (601.2h). Two conditions still have to be met:

1. An opponent must have lost life this turn. Merely attacking with Robber of the Rich isn't enough — the exile trigger only requires the defending player have more cards in hand. If Robber of the Rich's combat damage hasn't been dealt yet (e.g., Autumn is trying to cast Light Up the Stage in the declare attackers step) and no other life loss has occurred, spectacle isn't available and Autumn would have to pay {2}{R} instead — but note Light Up the Stage is a sorcery, so that timing wouldn't work anyway. I'm assuming Autumn casts it in a main phase after Robber of the Rich's damage or other life loss occurred; if no opponent has lost life at that point, the spectacle option simply doesn't exist. The amount of life lost and how many opponents lost life don't matter (Light Up the Stage ruling #7).
2. Normal timing applies. Spectacle doesn't change when you can cast the spell (Light Up the Stage ruling #8), and Robber of the Rich's permission is limited to a turn Autumn attacked with a Rogue. Since Light Up the Stage is a sorcery, Autumn must cast it during one of their own main phases with an empty stack.

Multiplayer note: the rules provided are framed around "an opponent" losing life, so with more than two players any one opponent's life loss turns spectacle on; Robber of the Rich's trigger and casting permission specifically concern the card exiled from the defending player Nehemiah's library.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

Robber of the Rich allows Autumn to cast the card and "may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." This changes how the player may pay a cost, and they can do so with any mana, regardless of color. 

"Spectacle" is an alternative cost ([702.137a]), and can only be used if no other alternative cost is being paid. Luckily, Robber of the Rich does not create an alternative cost, it just changes how mana may be spent.

entries.question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Jinx replaces the land type, causing Urza's Saga to lose its chapter abilities while still a Saga and thus be immediately sacrificed (so no Chapter III).
entries.answer:
Nico immediately sacrifices Urza's Saga. Jinx sets Urza's Saga's land subtype to a basic land type, so under rule 305.7 Urza's Saga loses all abilities generated from its rules text and its old land type — that includes its three chapter abilities — and gains the mana ability of the chosen basic type. It's still an enchantment with the Saga subtype (Jinx changes only land subtypes; card types and supertypes are unaffected per 205.4b), and the Saga state-based action then applies: a Saga with no chapter abilities is sacrificed right away, exactly as described for the Blood Moon case in Urza's Saga ruling #1. Rule 704.5s/714.4 handle this as a state-based action that doesn't use the stack, so it happens the next time a player would receive priority — no one can respond in between.

Notes:
- Because Urza's Saga is sacrificed at once, the third chapter never triggers, so Nico gets no artifact tutor. Chapter III would only have triggered when a third lore counter was put on it (at the beginning of Nico's precombat main phase per 505.4/703.4f), and Urza's Saga won't be around for that.
- Abilities granted to Urza's Saga by other effects are not removed by 305.7, and the chapter I/II abilities it granted itself are such granted abilities (Urza's Saga ruling #5) — but this is moot, since the permanent is sacrificed before it can be tapped for {C} or for the Construct token ability.
- Timing assumption: Jinx has finished resolving. Nothing changes if Jinx is cast at a different point in the turn; the sacrifice happens as soon as Jinx resolves, since the lore-counter count (2) already meets or exceeds the "final chapter number" of a Saga with no chapter abilities.
- This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; only Nico, as controller of Urza's Saga, performs the sacrifice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
In layer 4, Urza's Saga will have its land type overwritten as well as lose all of its chapter abilities. It will gain the abilities to tap for {C} and to create Construct tokens in layer 6, as those abilities are granted by a continuous effect that was generated when the previous chapter abilities resolved..

Because Urza's Saga has lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, per the Urza's Saga ruling "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed".

entries.question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
entries.reason: Both conclude suspending is not casting and therefore doesn't count toward Ethersworn Canonist's restriction, so Ada can suspend Shade of Trokair and then cast Divination (order matters).
entries.answer:
Yes — assuming Ada hasn't cast any nonartifact spell yet this turn, and that they do it in that order (suspend first, then cast Divination), both actions work.

Why: exiling a card with suspend is a special action, not casting. It doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to ([116.2f], [702.62a], [Shade of Trokair ruling #7]). So paying {W} to exile Shade of Trokair with three time counters does not make Ada a player who "has cast a nonartifact spell this turn," and Ethersworn Canonist's restriction stays switched off. Ada can then cast Divination ({2}{U}) normally during their main phase with an empty stack ([117.1a], [307.5]).

But the suspend action does check castability: Ada may take it only if they could begin to cast Shade of Trokair from hand at that moment, taking into account any effect that prohibits casting it ([116.2f], [702.62c], [601.3], [Shade of Trokair ruling #2]). Shade of Trokair is a creature, so this must be during Ada's main phase with an empty stack, and Ethersworn Canonist must not currently be prohibiting them.

Order matters: if Ada casts Divination first, Ethersworn Canonist then prohibits them from casting additional nonartifact spells, so they could no longer "begin to cast" Shade of Trokair — and therefore could not use suspend on it either. Also note that after casting Divination, Ada can't cast further nonartifact spells this turn; and later, when the last time counter is removed from Shade of Trokair, actually casting it that turn will require that Ethersworn Canonist isn't restricting them then ([Shade of Trokair ruling #5]).

This works the same at any player count — Ethersworn Canonist restricts each player individually, so other players' spells don't affect Ada's ability to suspend or cast.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Suspending a card is not casting a spell, so it does not count towards Ethersworn Canonist's restriction.

entries.question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
entries.reason: Both conclude it's legal because Inventors' Fair's activation legality (including the three-artifact check) is determined before payment, and Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana ability may be activated during payment to help pay the cost.
entries.answer:
Yes, it's legal. Asa announces the ability of Inventors' Fair (cost {4}, {T}, Sacrifice Inventors' Fair); the "three or more artifacts" restriction is checked at that moment, when Asa still controls Krark-Clan Ironworks and both Piston Sledge (three artifacts — Inventors' Fair itself is a land, not an artifact). Then, during payment, Asa activates Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana ability, sacrificing one Piston Sledge to add {C}{C}, and spends that toward the {4} generic portion.

Why this works:
- Rule 605.3a lets a player activate a mana ability whenever they're activating an ability that requires a mana payment, even in the middle of that activation — so Krark-Clan Ironworks can be used after the legality check.
- [Inventors' Fair ruling #2] confirms the artifact count is checked only as the ability is activated, not again on resolution. So losing an artifact afterward doesn't matter.
- Total cost is locked in at determination (601.2f) and paid at 601.2h; the sacrifice of Piston Sledge is a cost of Krark-Clan Ironworks' own mana ability, not a second use of one payment for two things, so rule 118.10 isn't violated.

Practical notes: {C}{C} from Krark-Clan Ironworks covers only 2 of the {4} generic, so Asa still needs {2} more from other sources — and Inventors' Fair can't be tapped for {C} because its {T} is part of this ability's cost (118.3, a tapped permanent can't be tapped again). Also, the payment includes sacrificing Inventors' Fair itself. Partial payments aren't allowed (601.2h); if Asa can't come up with the rest, the activation is illegal and reversed, with mana abilities reversible under 733.1.

This works the same regardless of the number of players; nothing here depends on player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The process for activating an ability is the same as the process for casting a spell. It must be legal to activate the ability in order to put it onto the stack. Mana abilities are only activated after the legality of activating the original ability has been checked.

entries.question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Psychogenic Probe triggers because Progenitus's replacement effect changes the discard into a shuffle, and that shuffle (caused by Pain) meets Psychogenic Probe's trigger.
entries.answer:
Yes — Psychogenic Probe triggers and deals 2 damage to Nico.

Why: Progenitus has the replacement ability "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." When Pain resolves and Nico discards Progenitus, that ability replaces the discard-to-graveyard event with revealing it and shuffling it into Nico's library. Psychogenic Probe reads "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library, this artifact deals 2 damage to that player." Progenitus's ability is an ability that caused Nico to shuffle their library, so Psychogenic Probe's triggered ability triggers, and since Nico is the player who shuffled, Nico takes the 2 damage — even though Amare controls Psychogenic Probe.

A couple of notes:
- Psychogenic Probe's ability triggers automatically on the shuffle event and then goes on the stack; it does nothing until it resolves (603.2g, 608.1).
- The shuffle actually happens here (it isn't itself prevented or replaced), which is what makes the trigger valid; if some effect had prevented the shuffle entirely, nothing would trigger (603.2g).
- Incidentally, Amare casting Pain targeting Nico, an opponent, is a crime for cards that care about that (700.13).
- This works the same regardless of the number of players; with more than two players only Nico (the player who shuffled) is damaged.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Progenitus's replacement effect changes the effect of Pain from "Nico discards a card, putting it into their graveyard" to "Nico reveals a card and shuffles it into their library". Pain still caused the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers.

entries.question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
entries.reason: The candidate is incorrect — Pir replaces the single loyalty counter with two and Doubling Season then doubles those to four, so the planeswalker gains four counters rather than one.
entries.answer:
Ajani, Mentor of Heroes gains exactly 1 loyalty counter — neither Doubling Season nor Pir, Imaginative Rascal applies.

Why: the [+1] in the ability's cost is paid by putting a loyalty counter on Ajani, Mentor of Heroes as a *cost*, not as the result of an effect. Doubling Season only doubles counters an *effect* would put on a permanent you control, and Doubling Season ruling #4 states this explicitly: planeswalkers entering the battlefield get double loyalty counters, but counters put on to pay a loyalty ability's cost are not doubled. Pir, Imaginative Rascal has the same limitation — its text is "If one or more counters *would be put* on a permanent your team controls," i.e., a replacement effect for counter-placement effects, not for cost payments. So Albert puts on a single loyalty counter.

Side note on the counters the ability actually distributes: the three +1/+1 counters from "Distribute three +1/+1 counters among one, two, or three target creatures you control" are put on by an effect, so both Doubling Season and Pir, Imaginative Rascal do apply there, and Albert (as the affected permanents' controller) chooses the order the two replacement effects are applied per rule 616.1a/616.1g. Applying Doubling Season first then Pir, Imaginative Rascal gives (N×2)+1 counters on a creature assigned N counters; applying Pir, Imaginative Rascal first gives (N+1)×2. Albert announces the distribution as he activates the ability, and each target must get at least one counter (Ajani, Mentor of Heroes ruling #1).

None of this depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games (APNAP order in 101.4 only matters if multiple players had to make simultaneous replacement-effect choices).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Four.

Activating a planeswalker ability includes paying the loyalty cost, which in this case means adding one loyalty counter. Doubling Season only replaces effects, which are the result of a spell or ability. However Pir, Imaginative Rascal replaces the original one loyalty counter with two, which Doubling Season can then replace with doubling the additional loyalty counters, resulting in a total of four.

entries.question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
entries.reason: The candidate rules that Nico controls Haru-Onna's ETB trigger and draws, but the reference states Nico couldn't legally put Domestication onto a creature entering at the same time (so the described situation can't occur), so the conclusions conflict.
entries.answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield trigger, so Nico draws the card.

Why: Show and Tell instructs each player to put a card onto the battlefield, and such an object enters under that player's control by default, so Haru-Onna enters under Aminah's control and Domestication enters under Nico's control (110.2a). Both enter the battlefield simultaneously as Show and Tell resolves, and Domestication enters already attached to Haru-Onna (303.4e). Domestication's "You control enchanted creature" is a control-changing continuous effect, applied in layer 2 of the characteristic/control determination, which happens immediately and continuously — there is no window in which Haru-Onna is on the battlefield without Nico controlling it (613.1b, 303.4e).

The controller of a triggered ability is the player who controlled the ability's source at the time it triggered (113.8, 603.3a). Since Haru-Onna is controlled by Nico the moment it is on the battlefield, Haru-Onna's "When this creature enters, draw a card" is controlled by Nico, and "draw a card" refers to that ability's controller — Nico draws.

Note that Aminah still owns the Haru-Onna card, and Aminah remains the controller of Show and Tell; ownership and control are separate (110.2a). Also note Haru-Onna's other ability, "Whenever you cast a Spirit or Arcane spell, you may return this creature to its owner's hand," would now trigger off Nico's Spirit/Arcane spells while Nico controls it, and would return the card to Aminah's hand as its owner.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, except that at a multiplayer table every other player also gets the Show and Tell option to put a permanent onto the battlefield under their own control (110.2a).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nico must choose a permanent that is already on the battlefield for the Domestication to enchant. They can't choose a permanent that is entering at the same time.

entries.question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly concludes Skyhunter Patrol survives by claiming Amani lacks Revolt, ignoring that the saga is sacrificed after its ability resolves, creating Revolt before Fatal Push resolves so the creature would be destroyed.
entries.answer:
Yes, Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, but Skyhunter Patrol will not be destroyed.

Targeting: Fatal Push says "Destroy target creature if it has mana value 2 or less." The mana-value restriction is not part of the targeting requirement, so Fatal Push may target any creature on the battlefield, including a mana value 4 creature like Skyhunter Patrol; the mana value is only checked on resolution ([Fatal Push ruling #3], and see [115.2] — creatures on the battlefield are legal targets).

Resolution: Skyhunter Patrol is still on the battlefield and still a creature, so it is a legal target and Fatal Push resolves ([608.2b]). Amani then follows the instructions in order ([608.2c]). Skyhunter Patrol's mana value is 4 ({2}{W}{W}). Since Amani does not have Revolt (no permanent left the battlefield under their control this turn), only the "mana value 2 or less" clause applies, and that condition is false, so nothing is destroyed. Fatal Push finishes resolving and is put into Amani's graveyard ([608.2n]). If Amani had Revolt, the 4-or-less clause would apply instead and Skyhunter Patrol would be destroyed.

Timing note on the copy: Founding the Third Path's chapter III exiles the instant or sorcery card, copies it, and lets Amani cast the copy — Amani must cast it right then, as the ability resolves, and must pay its costs ({B} for Fatal Push) ([Founding the Third Path ruling #2]). Also, because Fatal Push targets a creature an opponent controls, casting it that way is a crime ([700.13], [Crime]) if Skyhunter Patrol is controlled by an opponent; if Amani controls Skyhunter Patrol themselves, no crime is committed. This holds the same whether the game has two players or more — the only multiplayer wrinkle is that "opponent" for the crime check covers any of Amani's opponents ([700.13]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and it will be destroyed by Fatal Push.

Fatal Push does not check for the target's mana value when put on the stack, so Amani is allowed to target Skyhunter Patrol.

Amani will put Fatal Push on the stack as part of the resolution of Founding the Third Path's third chapter. Once the ability is done resolving, SBAs are checked and the saga is sacrificed. In particular this means that Amani will have Revolt when Fatal Push resolves, thus Skyhunter Patrol will get destroyed.

entries.question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Titania's Song's effects apply first, leaving Soldevi Digger as a 2/2 colorless artifact creature with no abilities, so Bludgeon Brawl does not affect it.
entries.answer:
After Titania's Song resolves, Soldevi Digger is a 2/2 colorless artifact creature named Soldevi Digger, with mana cost {2} (mana value 2), no subtypes, and no abilities at all — it is not an Equipment and has no equip ability and no "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library."

Why: both enchantments create continuous effects that are applied in layers (613.1a). Titania's Song is both a type-changing effect (layer 4), an ability-removing effect (layer 6), and a power/toughness-setting effect (layer 7b); Bludgeon Brawl is a type/subtype-changing effect (layer 4) and an ability-adding effect (layer 6). Within a layer, order is normally timestamp (613.7), but dependency overrides timestamps (613.8). Bludgeon Brawl only applies to "each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact," and Titania's Song's type change turns Soldevi Digger into an artifact creature, changing whether Bludgeon Brawl applies to it at all. Bludgeon Brawl is therefore dependent on Titania's Song, so Titania's Song is applied first even though it has the later timestamp.

Once Titania's Song has been applied, Soldevi Digger is an artifact creature, so it is no longer a legal object for Bludgeon Brawl to affect — Bludgeon Brawl grants it nothing (no Equipment subtype, no equip {2}, no "+X/+0" ability). Titania's Song's ability-removal strips Soldevi Digger's own {2} ability, and its power and toughness are each set to its mana value, 2 (613.6 shows how the pieces of one effect land in their own layers).

Color: Soldevi Digger's mana cost is {2}, which is generic mana with no colored symbols, so it remains colorless (105.2). Note Titania's Song's own text also says that if Titania's Song leaves the battlefield, its effect on Soldevi Digger continues until end of turn — that card text governs.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game since both enchantments affect artifacts regardless of controller.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities. Applying Titania's Song would cause Bludgeon Brawl to no longer apply (since Soldevi Digger would be a creature). However, applying Bludgeon Brawl would not change how Titania's Song's effect is applied, so Bludgeon Brawl is dependent on Titania's Song. Titania's Song applies first, and then Bludgeon Brawl won't affect Soldevi Digger since it's a creature.

entries.question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Enlarge ends and the -1/-1 counters remain so Goblin Piker dies in cleanup, and Baron Sengir survives and its death-trigger triggers.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: In the cleanup step, Goblin Piker dies, and Baron Sengir survives.

During combat damage: Goblin Piker, pumped by Enlarge, is 9/8 with trample; Baron Sengir with Grafted Exoskeleton is 7/7 with infect and is indestructible from Withstand Death. Because Baron Sengir has infect, its 7 combat damage to Goblin Piker isn't marked as damage — instead Audrey's Goblin Piker gets seven -1/-1 counters [702.90c]. At that moment Goblin Piker is 9/8 with seven -1/-1 counters, i.e. 2/1, so it survives. Goblin Piker's 9 damage to Baron Sengir is just marked damage, and Withstand Death makes Baron Sengir indestructible, so it isn't destroyed.

At the end of the turn, in the cleanup step, all damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn" effects end simultaneously [514.2]. That means the 9 damage marked on Baron Sengir goes away, its indestructible from Withstand Death ends, and Enlarge's +7/+7 and trample on Goblin Piker end. The seven -1/-1 counters are counters, not a duration effect, so they stay on Goblin Piker. Applying power/toughness changes in layer 7 [613.1g], Goblin Piker is base 2/1 with seven -1/-1 counters, i.e. -5/-6. Its toughness is 0 or less, so the state-based action puts it into Audrey's graveyard [704.5f]; regeneration and indestructible would not save it from a toughness-0 death anyway (as Withstand Death's own text notes).

Baron Sengir's triggered ability "Whenever a creature dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn dies, put a +2/+2 counter on Baron Sengir" has its trigger event (Goblin Piker dying) occur, so it will trigger. The provided rules here don't include the cleanup-step rule that governs an additional cleanup step when triggered abilities trigger there, so I can't cite the exact procedure, but once that trigger resolves Baron Sengir would be 5/5 base + one +2/+2 counter + Grafted Exoskeleton's +2/+2 = 9/9.

Timing note: I'm assuming both creatures dealt combat damage in the normal combat damage step and nothing else intervened. If Baron Sengir had somehow not dealt its damage, Goblin Piker would have no -1/-1 counters and would simply shrink back to 2/1 and live.

Player count: this interaction is entirely between Audrey's attacker and Nico's blocker, so it plays out the same whether the game has two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Enlarge wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker remain. Goblin Piker dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.

entries.question: Niko has a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] in their graveyard with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ashley controls [Containment Priest], and casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Niko. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Containment Priest causes Skullbriar to be exiled instead of entering the battlefield and that it retains its +1/+1 counters while in exile.
entries.answer:
Ghastly Conscription resolves, but every card it would manifest — including Skullbriar, the Walking Grave — is exiled instead by Containment Priest, and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its two +1/+1 counters in exile.

Step by step:

1. Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from Niko's graveyard in a face-down pile, shuffles that pile, then manifests those cards — i.e., puts them onto the battlefield face down as 2/2 creatures. Manifesting is not casting.
2. Containment Priest reads "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead." Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is a nontoken creature card and it wasn't cast (manifest puts it onto the battlefield directly), so Containment Priest's replacement effect applies and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave — and every other manifested card — is exiled instead of entering the battlefield. Containment Priest's ability only spares cards that were cast, even from unusual zones like a graveyard [Containment Priest ruling #1]. Because the pile was shuffled, it doesn't matter which order the cards were in; none of them arrive on the battlefield.
3. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's third ability says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is neither hand nor library, so the two +1/+1 counters stay on it. That ability has to function in the zone Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is moving from, and it does work from the graveyard [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]; it retains all kinds of counters, not just +1/+1 counters [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5]. Since +1/+1 counters affect its power and toughness even outside the battlefield, the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is 3/3 [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2].

Net result: Niko's graveyard is emptied of creature cards, nothing enters the battlefield, and Ashley's Ghastly Conscription accomplishes nothing beyond exiling Niko's graveyard creatures — with Skullbriar, the Walking Grave sitting in exile still carrying its two +1/+1 counters. If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave later returns to the battlefield from exile, it will still have those counters (though "as long as it has a counter" effects from its previous existence do not carry over) [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3].

The provided rules don't cover whether the exiled cards end up face down or face up, so I can't settle that detail. Ghastly Conscription targets a single player either way, so the outcome is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; only the chosen target player's graveyard is affected.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: In order for counters to remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, it needs to have that ability immediately before it changes zones. It did have that ability in the graveyard, so it is exiled face down with the +1/+1 counters remaining on it during that change. It then attempts to enter the battlefield, but remains in exile instead due to Containment Priest. Since it becomes a new object, it will be face-up in exile. However it didn't change zones, so the counters will remain on it in exile.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Putrid Leech became a new object when it stopped being revealed and was returned, so Skill Borrower grants a fresh instance of the ability and Ashley can activate it again.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ashley can activate the Putrid Leech ability granted by Skill Borrower a second time this turn.

Why: Skill Borrower says "Play with the top card of your library revealed" and grants Skill Borrower all activated abilities of that top card while it's an artifact or creature card. Putrid Leech's ability reads "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Activate only once each turn." That's a restriction printed on the granting object, and rule 602.5c says that when an object acquires an activated ability with a use restriction from another object, the restriction applies only to that ability as acquired from that object — it does not apply to other, identically worded abilities.

The key step is rule 401.6: if a player is playing with the top card of their library revealed and that particular card stops being revealed for any length of time before being revealed again, it becomes a new object. When Ashley used Sensei's Divining Top's first ability ({1}: look at the top three and put them back in any order) to put Putrid Leech second from the top, that card stopped being revealed. Putting it back on top with the second activation makes it a new object. So Skill Borrower is now granted the ability from a different object, and the "Activate only once each turn" restriction from the earlier object no longer limits it.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the sequence as given — the first Putrid Leech activation fully happened before Sensei's Divining Top shuffled the card off the top and back. Note also that the second Sensei's Divining Top activation described here is its first ability again ({1}), not the {T} draw ability, since tapping it would move Sensei's Divining Top itself to the top of the library. If instead the top card had never left the revealed position (for example, the three cards were put back in the same order), it would still be the same object and the once-per-turn restriction would still block a second activation.

One related caution from Skill Borrower's rulings: if the top card changes while Ashley is in the middle of activating a granted ability, the ability is still activated and resolves normally even though Skill Borrower has lost it (Skill Borrower ruling #4), and rule 401.5 means a new top card isn't revealed or lookable until the activation is finished.

This answer doesn't depend on player count; nothing here involves other players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Putrid Leech stopped being revealed for a time, so it is no longer the same object that it was before. Skill Borrower has a new ability that just has the same text as the ability that was activated earlier.

entries.question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Spider Umbra is destroyed as it replaces the creature's destruction and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders survives. With Spider Umbra attached it's a 2/2, so Yamabushi's Flame's 3 damage is lethal and Mons's Goblin Raiders would be destroyed — but umbra armor replaces that: all damage marked on Mons's Goblin Raiders is removed and Spider Umbra is destroyed instead [702.89a]. This is mandatory, not optional [Spider Umbra ruling #6], and applies regardless of why Mons's Goblin Raiders would be destroyed [Spider Umbra ruling #4].

Because Mons's Goblin Raiders is never destroyed, it never dies, so Yamabushi's Flame's exile clause ("If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead") never gets an event to replace. Note it's the game's lethal-damage rules, not Yamabushi's Flame itself, that cause Spider Umbra to be destroyed here [Spider Umbra ruling #0]. Spider Umbra goes to Noah's graveyard; Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield as a 1/1 with no damage marked on it, and it does not have toughness 0 or less, so no state-based action puts it into the graveyard [704.5f].

Assumed timing: the damage from Yamabushi's Flame is what would destroy Mons's Goblin Raiders, and damage results are processed with replacement effects applying at that moment [120.4c, 614.1]. If instead Mons's Goblin Raiders had already been dealt damage earlier this turn and were destroyed by that, the outcome is the same: umbra armor removes all marked damage and Spider Umbra is destroyed. Also, later in the turn Mons's Goblin Raiders is no longer protected — Yamabushi's Flame's exile-instead effect would still apply if that same damage source's shield were relevant, but since Spider Umbra is gone, a second lethal damage event would simply kill (or exile, if from Yamabushi's Flame) Mons's Goblin Raiders.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count — it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Spider Umbra is destroyed and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.

There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the same event. Umbra armor is attempting to replace the destruction of the creature, while Yamabushi's Flame's effect is attempting to replace where the creature moves to. The "move to the graveyard" event is a part of the "destroy" event, so the umbra armor replacement effect must apply first. Once that effect has been applied, the creature is no longer about to die, so there are no more effects to apply.

If the Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later in the turn, the Yamabushi's Flame's replacement effect will apply at that time and cause it to move to exile instead of the graveyard.

entries.question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate agrees that Carrion Grub is shuffled into Alex's library but diverges from the reference by leaving companion-announce legality unresolved rather than stating Alex cannot have Kaheera as companion because Carrion Grub is in the starting deck.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: The game immediately ends with no winner or loser, and everyone still in it starts a new game — and Carrion Grub, which Alex brought in from the sideboard with Wish, is part of Alex's library for that new game. Kaheera, the Orphanguard, if Alex never took the special action to put it into their hand, never became involved in the game, so it stays outside the game (sideboard).

Details:

1. Restarting: Karn Liberated's −14 ability ends the current game instantly; no player wins, loses, or draws it, and all players still in the game begin a new game using the rule 103 starting procedure [727.1], [104.6], [Karn Liberated ruling #12]. Nothing from the old game carries over [Karn Liberated ruling #1], and no player has counters or emblems [Karn Liberated ruling #10]. Karn Liberated's ability finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, leaving its exiled non-Aura permanent cards in exile and then putting them onto the battlefield under Alex's control; any resulting triggers go on the stack at the first upkeep [727.4], [Karn Liberated ruling #4].

2. Carrion Grub: All cards involved in the ended game are involved in the new game, even cards that weren't originally in it, and ownership doesn't change. Rule 727.2 gives exactly this example (a creature card brought in from outside the game with Living Wish): the card is part of that player's library when the new game begins [727.2]. So Carrion Grub, brought in via Wish, is shuffled into Alex's library for the new game — it is no longer a sideboard card. (Only cards an effect specifically exempts from the restart procedure aren't in their owner's deck [727.5].)

3. Kaheera, the Orphanguard: A companion begins the game outside the game (your sideboard in tournament play) [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #10], and it only enters the game once you take the special action of paying {3} to put it into your hand [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #14], after which it behaves like any other card in the game [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #11]. Assuming Alex never paid the {3}, Kaheera, the Orphanguard was never "involved in the game," so rule 727.2 doesn't pull it into the new game's library; it remains outside the game. If instead Alex had already put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into their hand before the restart, it was involved in the game and would begin the new game in Alex's library under [727.2].

4. What the provided rules do NOT settle: whether Alex may announce a companion again for the new game, and how that interacts with the fact that Alex's new starting deck now contains Carrion Grub (an Insect, which is not a Cat, Elemental, Nightmare, Dinosaur, or Beast). Companion is checked against your starting deck after setting aside sideboard cards [702.139b], and the reveal happens before shuffling your deck into your library [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #0], but no rule here tells us how that pregame step is handled during a restart. Treat that part as unresolved rather than assuming either outcome.

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, every player still in the game when it restarts joins the new game; anyone who had already left does not [Karn Liberated ruling #11], and in a limited-range-of-influence multiplayer game all players are involved regardless of range of influence [727.7]. Otherwise the answer is the same at two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Carrion Grub will be shuffled into Alex's library along with the rest of the cards in the game. Because Carrion Grub violates Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion restriction, Alex can't announce it as their companion for the restarted game.
